query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Using a replica-exchange molecular dynamics framework combined with thermodynamic integration to sample alloy composition and temperature space will accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy samples in their solid phase near melting conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a free-energy sampling scheme based on replica-exchange molecular dynamics integrated with thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed at high-temperature regimes approaching melting for a diverse range of high-entropy alloy compositions, calibrated against design benchmarks obtained from high-precision calorimetric experiments and binary/ternary alloy data.
generation.structural_mediator: The accurate mapping of the free-energy landscape through enhanced temperature and compositional sampling mediates the prediction of phase transitions and melting-related thermodynamic properties.
generation.mechanism: Replica-exchange molecular dynamics efficiently traverses the complex configurational space of high-entropy alloys, while thermodynamic integration computes the free-energy differences associated with phase transitions. This combination captures the atomic-scale fluctuations and structural reorganizations that govern melting behavior and associated thermodynamic parameters.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will predict melting temperatures and associated thermodynamic properties with an accuracy within approximately 5% of the experimental calorimetric benchmarks.
generation.baseline: Current simplified models and standard MD techniques that often suffer from limited sampling of compositional complexity and temperature-driven fluctuations.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be reliable for high-entropy alloys with compositions that do not undergo severe phase segregation or decomposition prior to melting. Its applicability under extreme compositional or kinetic conditions remains to be fully validated.
generation.uncertainty: While the technique shows promise, uncertainties remain regarding its performance for alloys with exceptionally complex phase behavior or non-equilibrium structural states, which may affect precise quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a set of replica-exchange molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration simulations across a range of high-entropy alloy compositions. Compare the predicted melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting with high-precision calorimetric measurements for the same alloys.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulated values deviate by more than 5% consistently from the experimental measurements over a statistically significant set of alloy compositions, the proposed approach would be considered falsified.

The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
